one_line_rationale: Strong customer demand exists around reducing dinner mental load and grocery waste, but high pantry-tracking friction and low willingness to pay require prototype testing before building.
markdown:
# PantryPal discovery brief

## 1. Recommendation
We recommend testing further before committing engineering resources to build the core app. Research confirms that busy working households experience daily decision fatigue and discard spoiled food [P01:t2, P02:t2, P04:t2, S01]. However, five different participants explicitly stated that entering pantry inventories manually causes immediate churn, creating a major feasibility risk for the core value proposition [P02:t8, P05:t8, P07:t8, P08:t8, P10:t8]. Furthermore, stated willingness to pay is low, centering between free and a few euros per month [P01:t9, P02:t9, P03:t9, P04:t9, P05:t9, P10:t9, S05]. We must test lightweight onboarding and meal-plan modification before full product development [UNSUPPORTED].

## 2. Who the users are
The primary user segment consists of busy multi-person households and working parents who cook at home on weeknights [P01, P02, P04, idea_brief]. A secondary segment includes cost-sensitive single parents managing strict grocery budgets [P03]. In contrast, university students living alone cook infrequently and rely on convenience options [P07:t1]. Similarly, retired couples maintain decades-old stable routines without needing planning apps [P09:t1]. Shared flatmates face coordination issues, but they cook independently rather than sharing communal dinners [P10:t1]. Solo individuals and freelance couples with unpredictable hours feel constrained by rigid meal plans [P05:t1, P07:t1].

## 3. Problems that are real
Dinner decision fatigue is a daily pain point for primary household cooks [P01:t2, P03:t2, P04:t2, S04]. Adults spend an average of 22 minutes each day deciding what to cook [S04]. Household food waste is frequent and causes financial and emotional distress [P01:t2, P01:t4, P02:t2, P03:t2, P05:t2, S01]. European households discard approximately 19% of the food they buy [S01]. Dual-shopper households experience uncoordinated purchasing, resulting in duplicate ingredients that spoil [P02:t2, P02:t4, P04:t4, P10:t2]. Rigid planning attempts frequently fail when plans are interrupted by busy schedules or missing ingredients [P01:t3, P03:t4, P05:t4].

## 4. What the evidence says
Evidence across 9 usable interviews demonstrates that meal-planning friction is behavioral, whereas interview P06 must be discounted due to leading interviewer questions [P01, P02, P03, P04, P05, P06:t1, P06:t8, P07, P08, P09, P10].

### Actual behaviors
Busy parents resort to repetitive fallback meals when plans collapse at the end of the day [P01:t3]. Households track groceries through ad-hoc methods such as notes apps, shared list tools, or paper pads on the fridge [P01:t6, P02:t6, P03:t6, P04:t6, P10:t6]. Shoppers glance casually into refrigerators before shopping and forget what they already have [P02:t5, P08:t5, P10:t5]. When an ingredient is missing, planned dinners fall apart and cause expensive emergency takeout purchases [P02:t3, P03:t4].

### Stated preferences and requirements
Participants demand that setup require negligible friction, warning: "Setup has to be fast. If I need to type in my whole pantry I'll quit on day two" [P02:t8, P05:t8, P07:t8, P08:t8, P10:t8]. Users insist on autonomy over the schedule: "I want to edit the plan easily. I don't want an app dictating to me" [P01:t8, P02:t8, P03:t8, P05:t8]. Recipes must fit constrained schedules: "Recipes must be realistic for weeknights. Thirty minutes at most" [P01:t8, P04:t8]. Family cooks require personalisation for household diets: "It would need to understand allergies and what we actually like, otherwise it's just noise" [P03:t8, P04:t8].

### Willingness to pay
Stated willingness to pay is modest, typically capped at a few euros per month or dependent on grocery savings [P01:t9, P02:t9, P04:t9, P10:t9]. Median stated willingness to pay across consumers is EUR 3.50 per month [S05]. Multiple participants refuse to pay for planning tools and expect a free or ad-supported model [P03:t9, P05:t9, P07:t9, P09:t9]. One extreme outlier offered thirty euros a month following a massive spoilage disaster, but this is an unrepresentative exception [P08:t2, P08:t9].

## 5. Competitors and market
The European Household Food Panel found two-person households spend an average of EUR 118 weekly on groceries [S02]. In the broader market, only 11% of households currently use a meal-planning app [S03]. Direct competitors address individual slices of the workflow but leave gaps:
- MealLoop targets families with weekly plans and grocery lists for EUR 6.99/month or EUR 49.99/year, but does not track current pantry inventory [C:MealLoop].
- PlanPlate offers calendar sharing and recipe importing for EUR 2.99/month to couples and flatmates [C:PlanPlate].
- PantryGenie tracks pantry inventory with barcode scanning and expiry alerts for EUR 3.99/month, but lacks automated dinner planning [C:PantryGenie].
- FridgeChef generates recipes from fridge photos with an ad-supported free tier and EUR 4.99/month premium tier, but does not provide weekly dinner planning [C:FridgeChef].
- SupperSync provides shared dinner scheduling, chore assignment, and list sharing for EUR 4.49/month per household [C:SupperSync].
- WeekWise offers budget plans for free with a EUR 29.99 recipe pack [C:WeekWise].
- ZeroWaste Kitchen offers donation-supported use-it-up recipes for leftover ingredients without structured planning [C:ZeroWaste Kitchen].

## 6. Risks and open assumptions
- Feasibility and adoption risk: Users refuse to log inventory manually, creating severe abandonment risk during onboarding [P02:t8, P05:t8, P08:t8, P10:t8].
- Value risk: Automated meal plans fail if users feel micromanaged or cannot easily swap out meals on weeknights [P01:t8, P02:t8, P05:t8].
- Monetization risk: Customer willingness to pay is low, and prices above competitor baselines of EUR 2.99 to EUR 4.99 will encounter steep resistance [C:PlanPlate, C:PantryGenie, C:FridgeChef, S05].
- Retention risk: Irregular schedules and unexpected dining out disrupt rigid plans, leading users to abandon planning apps completely [P05:t1, P05:t4].
- Grocery sync friction: Only 4% of grocery purchases were made online according to historic data, meaning shopping list execution happens primarily in physical stores [S09].

## 7. What to test next
1. Wizard-of-Oz pantry onboarding test: Test whether households will complete onboarding using a 30-second fridge photo scan or quick-tap staple checklist instead of manual data entry [UNSUPPORTED]. Target onboarding completion rate of 65% across 40 recruit households [UNSUPPORTED].
2. Interactive plan-flexibility prototype: Test whether users engage with an interactive weekly plan where dinners can be swapped in under 30 seconds [UNSUPPORTED]. Target an 80% plan-retention rate across 30 busy households over a 5-day trial [UNSUPPORTED].
3. Fake-door pricing test: Run targeted landing pages displaying value propositions and subscription tiers at EUR 2.99/month and EUR 4.99/month [UNSUPPORTED]. Target a minimum call-to-action click-through rate of 5% across 500 visitors per variant [UNSUPPORTED].

## 8. Unsupported or weak claims
- The claim that 97% of households would pay for automated meal planning is an unsubstantiated blog assertion contradicted by interview data [P03:t9, P05:t9, P07:t9, P09:t9, S08].
- The stat asserting 73% of families struggle with dinner decisions lacks attribution and year [S07].
- The market growth rate of 25% annually provides no source or year [S06].
- The 4% online grocery purchase stat originates from an outdated 2016 review and may not represent current behavior [S09].
- Interview P06 consists entirely of leading questions and agreeable prompts, rendering its affirmations invalid as independent customer evidence [P06:t1, P06:t2, P06:t8, P06:t9].
- The assumption that households will diligently update an app when food is consumed has no supporting evidence in the data [UNSUPPORTED].
